## Why I took this module seriously

Coming in with three years of full-stack experience, my instinct was that a
portfolio module would be an easy win. **It wasn't** and that's exactly why
it was valuable. Writing for a reader who isn't already sold on my work is a
different discipline than writing production code.

## Skills I actively built

### Git beyond `git push -f`
In a team I already use feature branches, but for a solo project I was guilty
of bulk commits. Forcing myself into **small, message-driven commits** here
surfaced a habit that translates directly to code review quality at work.

### Quarto as a documentation platform
I've written Markdown for README files for years, but Quarto's **executable
code blocks**, **cross-references**, and **SCSS theming** turned what would
have been a static page into a reproducible artefact. `quarto render`
regenerates every chart from scratch — no stale screenshots.

### SCSS and design systems
Full-stack work pushed me to rely on component libraries. Writing raw SCSS for
this site — Sass variables, `@import` Google Fonts, gradient title text —
reminded me how much leverage there is in a well-chosen design token.

### Technical writing
Writing the [Sales Analytics](projects/sales-analytics/index.qmd) project
taught me that good analysis is mostly about **framing the question** clearly
before writing any code. That skill matters in engineering RFCs too.

## Challenges I overcame

::: {.callout-warning title="Biggest friction points"}
- **Quarto's `_quarto.yml` indentation** YAML doesn't forgive mistakes, and
  debugging a silent-failing navbar took an hour the first time.
- **GitHub Pages caching** — forgetting `.nojekyll` cost me a confused evening
  of "why is my CSS missing?".
- **Balancing design and substance**  it's tempting to spend a whole day on
  colour palettes. I set myself a rule: substance first, polish last.
:::

## How this connects to my career

The habits this module enforced  **incremental Git history**, **executable
documentation**, **branded personal presence** - are the same habits that
separate senior engineers from mid-level ones. I already applied the
executable-docs idea to a runbook at work the week I wrote the first project.

## What I would do differently

1. Start a **daily commit journal** from day one instead of catching up.
2. Write **tests for my sample Python code** so the site fails loudly if a
   library upgrade breaks a chart.
3. Add a **blog** section to turn one-off learnings into public posts.
